stories.headline: Update: Houthi Rebels Kill Six in Missile Strike on Vessel in Bab el-Mandeb Strait
stories.summary:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels fired three ballistic missiles at a Yemeni commercial vessel in the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Tuesday, killing six people, including four crew members and two members of government-allied National Resistance Forces, Yemeni authorities said. It is the first confirmed lethal Houthi attack on shipping during the current round of fighting, marking a significant escalation in the region's maritime crisis.

The strike comes as the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed by Iran, heightening global attention on the Bab el-Mandeb as an alternate oil export route for Saudi Arabia. Houthis have simultaneously intensified attacks on government-held port city Mokha on the Red Sea and on Saudi oil facilities, raising fears of a broader regional conflagration and the reignition of Yemen's civil war after its 2022 truce.

Houthi chief negotiator Mohammed Abdul-Salam said the group is open to negotiations but demanded the lifting of a Saudi-led blockade imposed in 2015. The escalation opens a new front in the Middle East conflict and threatens global energy shipping at a moment when alternative routes are already under pressure from the Hormuz crisis.

stories.headline: Putin Threatens Retaliation Against EU Over Planned Seizure of Russian Ships
stories.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday threatened direct retaliation if European Union member states move to seize Russian commercial vessels, labeling any such action "piracy." Putin warned that Moscow would respond "wherever necessary" to protect Russian cargo ships, sharply escalating diplomatic tensions between Russia and the West over sanctions enforcement.

The threat comes as EU governments have been exploring asset seizure measures targeting Russian shipping as part of broader sanctions packages tied to the ongoing war in Ukraine. The standoff introduces a new dimension to the Russia-West conflict, potentially putting commercial maritime traffic at risk on multiple seas.

Putin's remarks represent one of his most direct warnings aimed at European economic measures and signal that Moscow views ship seizures as a red line warranting military or retaliatory action. Analysts note the statement could complicate European legal and logistical efforts to enforce sanctions while raising the specter of incidents at sea involving Russian-flagged or Russian-cargo vessels.

stories.headline: New Zealand Prime Minister Luxon Survives Second Leadership Challenge Ahead of November Election
stories.summary:
New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon survived a second internal vote of confidence within four months on Wednesday, emerging from a three-hour caucus meeting to declare he has the "full support" of the ruling National Party. The challenge followed a series of public missteps, including an uncoordinated suggestion of a referendum on the country's electoral system and a speech that alienated small business owners, drawing widespread backlash.

Luxon's preferred prime minister rating has fallen to a record-low 17% according to a 1News Verian poll released Wednesday, though he still leads all other candidates in the survey. Unemployment has risen to an 11-year high of 5.6%, and sluggish economic growth has eroded support for a leader who came to office in the 2023 election on a cost-of-living platform.

New Zealand holds its next general election on November 7, giving Luxon little time to rebuild his standing. His survival of Wednesday's challenge keeps the National Party's leadership intact for now, but analysts note that persistent polling weakness and continued economic stagnation could make his position precarious as the campaign approaches.

stories.headline: Update: Colombia Earthquake Death Toll Rises Above 180 as Rescue Crews Race to Free Trapped Survivors
stories.summary:
Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock following Monday's magnitude 7.4 earthquake, with the confirmed death toll standing at 181 and an aggregated figure from local officials suggesting it may exceed 240. The quake struck at 7:34 a.m. local time and was felt across hundreds of miles of western Colombia, with the cities of Cali and Pereira suffering the worst damage. President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a state of emergency and reported nearly 2,600 injuries, approximately 200 people still missing, more than 1,100 homes destroyed, and more than 8,000 damaged.

In Cali, a city of 2.2 million, 95 deaths have been confirmed and 239 people remain trapped across 45 buildings that have fully or partially collapsed. Several floors of a hospital dedicated in part to pediatric care collapsed, and a school collapse in the Calima neighborhood killed four children and seriously injured dozens more. Cali's mayor has imposed a nighttime curfew to prevent looting.

In Pereira, 79 deaths have been confirmed by the city's fire department. Authorities have implemented a car-free day to facilitate search operations, and hundreds of volunteers are working alongside emergency personnel to clear rubble. More than 70 aftershocks have been recorded since Monday, with two of magnitude 3.6 occurring early Tuesday, complicating rescue efforts.

This is a material update on the Colombia earthquake, which was first reported as having surpassed 200 deaths in a previous edition. Today's coverage introduces new figures from city-level officials, updated missing-persons counts, confirmed aftershock totals, and details on school and hospital collapses not previously reported.

stories.headline: Zhu Rongji, Chinese Premier Who Engineered WTO Entry and State-Enterprise Overhaul, Dies at 98
stories.summary:
Zhu Rongji, who served as China's premier from 1998 to 2003, has died at the age of 98. He was one of the most consequential economic architects in modern Chinese history, overseeing the country's accession to the World Trade Organization in 2001 and pushing through sweeping reforms of state-owned enterprises that cost tens of millions of workers their jobs while transforming China into the world's leading manufacturing power.

As vice premier and then premier under President Jiang Zemin, Zhu presided over a period of wrenching structural adjustment that dismantled the socialist-era iron rice bowl system of guaranteed state employment. His reforms, while enormously disruptive to workers, helped lay the foundation for China's explosive economic growth in the two decades that followed.

Zhu was widely regarded within China and internationally as a technocratic reformer with a blunt communication style uncommon among senior Communist Party officials. His death marks the passing of a pivotal figure from the generation of leaders who shaped post-Mao China's integration into the global economy.

stories.headline: DHS Plans to Equip ICE Officers With Electric-Shock Gloves at Cost of Up to $20 Million
stories.summary:
The Department of Homeland Security published a notice outlining plans to spend up to $20 million equipping Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers with gloves capable of delivering painful electric shocks. The devices, called the Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter (G.L.O.V.E.) and manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky, are intended to gain compliance from combative individuals during arrests or detentions. According to the manufacturer, the shock is typically effective in bringing individuals into compliance in under three seconds, and DHS aims to have thousands of the devices deployed by March.

Supporters of the program argue that such tools provide officers with a less-lethal option for subduing resistant individuals, potentially reducing the risk of injury to both officers and detainees compared with more aggressive physical force. Critics, including civil liberties advocates, have raised concerns about the potential for abuse, particularly in the context of immigration enforcement operations that have already drawn scrutiny over detainee treatment.

The announcement comes amid broader debate over ICE enforcement tactics and the conditions under which detained migrants are held. The notice was published Monday and represents a formal procurement action, meaning the plan is materially advanced beyond a policy proposal.

stories.headline: Severe Derecho Cuts Power to 500,000 in Chicago Region, Tornadoes Touch Down, Lightning Injures 16 at Ohio Prison
stories.summary:
A powerful storm system swept from Iowa through Indiana on Tuesday, knocking out power to more than half a million people in the Chicago area and northwestern Indiana. The National Weather Service confirmed two tornadoes touched down just south of Chicago, and the Storm Prediction Center said the intense system met the criteria for a derecho — a widespread, long-lived wind storm — after wind gusts of up to 99 mph were recorded in Gary, Indiana, with numerous other locations reporting gusts above 80 mph.

All flights were temporarily halted at Chicago's two major airports, O'Hare and Midway, as the storm passed through, causing a significant backlog of departures and arrivals. Widespread damage was reported across the region, including flooded roads, downed trees, and homes with structural damage. At least one death was reported in Ohio as the system moved east.

At the Grafton Reintegration Center southwest of Cleveland, lightning struck a group of incarcerated individuals returning from an evening meal, hospitalizing 16 people, one of whom was airlifted. The Ohio Department of Corrections said conditions were not immediately known for all those hospitalized. Utility crews were working to restore power, but large numbers of customers faced extended outages into Wednesday.
